ANP is released from the atria in response to high blood pressure and acts on the kidneys to decrease Na reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct. This increases urine volume and decreases blood volume therefore decreasing blood pressure.  Aldosterone is secreted by the adrenal gland in response to low blood pressure and acts on the kidneys to increase Na reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct. This increases blood volume and decreases blood pressure. ADH is released from the hypothalamus in response to increased plasma osmolality (often caused by high blood glucose levels) and acts on the kidney to increase water absorption in the collecting duct and loop of henle. This increases urine volume and decreases osmolality of the extracellular fluid, thus decreasing blood osmolality and increasing blood volume.  The release of ANP from the atria and ADH from the hypothalamus are regulated by baroreceptors which respond to changes in blood pressure.  Aldosterone is regulated by the renin-angiotensin system which is stimulated by decreased blood volume and decreased Na levels in the blood.  A good way to remember this is ANP=High Blood Pressure(HBP)Aldosterone=Low Blood Pressure(LBP)ADH=High Osmolarity(Hypernatraemia)  I have used the information from Dr Johnson's lecture on Renal Control of Fluid Balance in Case 12 and the Renal Physiology plenary in PCS 1. The primary pathological mechanism behind psychotic episodes is thought to be due to increased activation of D2 dopamine receptors, particularly the mesolimbic pathway which projects from the substantia nigra to the ventral tegmental area (VTA). This increased activation of dopaminergic neurons projecting to the nucleus accumbens causes a cascade of events resulting in hypofunctioning of the dorsal prefrontal cortex. This hypofunctioning of the dorsal PFC results in hyperactivation of subcortical structures such as the hippocampus and amygdala causing a breakdown in cognitive functioning as well as perception. I also focused on this particular example because often patients who exhibit psychotic symptoms have a history of personality disorders or comorbidity with other mental health issues which can make the diagnosis more difficult. Grave's disease is an autoimmune condition where the immune system makes antibodies against thyrotropin releasing hormone (TRH). Carbimazole is used to treat hypothyroidism and Graves disease. It is converted into methimazole which inhibits thyroid peroxidase. 1 hour old newborns are generally checked by doctors to see if they have spina bifida which occurs due to failure of closure of the neural tube. Neural tube formation is caused by induction of the mesodermal cells of the primitive streak by the notochord and epidermis.  Spina bifida occulta is a common benign form of spina bifida where only the dura mater is open leading to a small tuft of hair being visible between the scapulae. It is thought that this occurs when the closure of the neural tube does not meet at the bottom of the caudal region of the embryo.  Spina bifida aperta is a more severe type of spina bifida where there is incomplete formation of the vertebrae as well as opening of the dural lining (covering of the spinal cord). It leads to paralysis and other complications. The exact causes of spina bifida aperta are unclear but it has been linked with vitamin B9 (folate) and Wnt proteins.  More information can be found in Dr Wilson's lecture on 'Formation of the neural tube and cytokinesis'. Scaphoid fractures are common, particularly in young adults who fall onto an outstretched hand. They often occur at night as people fall from their beds, hence why they are known colloquially as 'midnight breakages'. It is very important that these fractures are treated well as there is a high risk of non-union if they are not. This is because the scaphoid is avascular i.e. it receives no blood supply from the proximal portion of the radius. New blood vessels must grow down the bone from the distal end to keep the bone nourished. If the fracture is immobilised too much then this will stop new vessels growing into the proximal part of the bone and so it will die. If not enough weight is allowed on the bone then the new blood vessels may not grow down the bone either. Therefore, it is important to find the right balance between immobilisation and allowing weight bearing to ensure the scaphoid heals well. A cast is usually used to immobilise the wrist for 6 weeks. X rays are taken regularly in this time to see how the fracture is healing. If there is any doubt about the fracture healing then a bone scan may be needed. Most scaphoid fractures heal with no problems but some do fail to unite. Non-union can occur up to two years after the initial injury. There are many reasons why a scaphoid fracture might fail to heal including: • How the fracture was managed.• How well the patient has followed the instructions.• The age of the patient.• Smoking.• Other medical conditions.• Whether the fracture was stable or unstable.• The type of scaphoid fracture.If a scaphoid fracture fails to heal a bone scan is usually arranged to confirm that there is no union. An MRI scan can also be useful to check the soft tissues around the scaphoid.Once a diagnosis of non-union has been made then various options can be considered. These include non surgical management and surgery.The decision of what is best depends on many factors including:• Age.• Occupation.• Hobbies.• Sport.• General health.• Patient preference.Non-operative treatment

Urea breath test can be used to detect infection by Helicobacter pylori, the main cause of peptic ulcers. It is positive if there is more than 10 mg of urea in the sample. 12-18 hours after ingestion of a radioactive form of urea, if there is an infection then most of the urea will have been absorbed into the blood from the stomach and exhaled via the lungs. In this case, there will be measurable amounts of urea in the expired air.  Normally less than 1mg of urea is detectable in the expired air.  The presence of urea in the expired air suggests that the bacteria has penetrated the epithelial cells of the stomach wall. This allows the urea to enter the circulatory system. The urea is then transported across the basolateral membrane of the parietal cells (by UTAT) and enters the lumen of the stomach. From here it is absorbed by the circulation and exhaled by the lungs.  In the absence of an infection, no urea should be detected in the expired air.  The sensitivity of the test is about 95% and the specificity is about 75%.   Source: Applied immunology tutorial, case 13. 'Infections caused by Helicobacter Pylori'.  Also, http://www.patient.co.uk/doctor/urea-breath-test-for-helicobacter-pylori-infection.  And http://www.health.harvard.edu/fhg/diagnostics/ubt.shtml.  I've put this question in the form of an explanation generation question because it requires you to think about how the urea breath test works and why the results may be different depending on whether or not someone has an infection.
